lessons.t: From prompt writing to context design
lessons.html:
Prompt engineering treated the prompt as a piece of prose you polish. In a production feature, the text a person writes is a small share of what the model reads. The rest is assembled by code on every call: tool definitions, retrieved passages, conversation history, earlier tool results, user profile fields, format instructions. Context engineering is the design of that assembly. It decides what goes in, in what order, at what size, and what gets dropped when the budget runs out.

The shift matters because the model has no other input. Given a fixed model, every quality difference between two calls comes from the tokens in front of it. If a support assistant gives a wrong refund answer, the cause is almost always one of five things in the assembled context, and only one of them is the wording of the instructions.

Context failureWhat it looks likeTypical fix
MissingThe fact or policy needed was never retrieved or passed inRetrieval, a tool, or a required field in the assembly
Wrong or staleAn outdated policy doc outranks the current oneFreshness filters, provenance, source ranking (Chapter 7)
Too muchThe right passage is present but buried among 40 othersSmaller top-k, reranking, summarised history
ConflictingSystem prompt says one thing, a retrieved doc or old turn says anotherA stated precedence rule; remove the loser
Badly framedInstructions are vague, or the task is never stated plainlyRewrite the instructions and add examples (next lesson)

What the model sees per call

Ask engineering for the assembled context of one real request, printed in full. Most teams have never read one. In a typical in-product assistant (illustrative numbers) you might find 1,500 tokens of system prompt, 6,000 tokens of tool definitions for 25 tools the request never uses, 9,000 tokens of retrieved chunks, 4,000 tokens of history and a 40-token user question. The question is 0.2% of the input. That ratio is a design decision, usually made by accident.

Treat each slot of the context as a component with an owner, a source, a token budget, a position and a refresh rule. That turns “improve the prompt” into concrete work: cut the tool list to the eight tools this surface needs, cap retrieval at 3,000 tokens, replace raw history older than ten turns with a summary, move the user’s plan tier from a retrieved doc into a structured field.

Order is a decision

Position affects both quality and cost. Stable material (instructions, tool definitions, reference docs) goes first so prompt caching can reuse it. Variable material (the latest turn, fresh retrieval) goes last. Lesson 5 covers the economics; Lesson 3 covers why placement inside a long context changes what the model notices.

Context engineering is also where most of the levers from the Chapter 1 behaviour-change ladder actually sit. Rungs 1 to 3 (instructions, examples, context and tools) are all context changes. They are quick to try, cheap to reverse and measurable against a fixed eval, which is why they come before model swaps and fine-tuning.

What changes for you

  • Before any quality review, read the fully assembled context for three failing cases. Diagnose which of the five failures caused each one before anyone edits wording.
  • Specify context as slots with budgets, sources and order. Lesson 6’s deliverable template is the format.
  • Treat “the prompt” as code that assembles context. It needs version control, review and an eval run on every change (Chapter 5).

lessons.t: System prompts, examples and structured outputs that hold up
lessons.html:
Three tools do most of the work of steering a fixed model: the system prompt, a handful of examples, and a schema for the output. Each fails in a predictable way when overused.

System prompts at the right altitude

Anthropic’s guidance describes two failure modes. One is brittle, hard-coded if-else logic that tries to anticipate every case. The other is vague guidance that assumes the model shares context it doesn’t have. Good system prompts sit between them. They state the role, the goal, who the user is, the constraints that matter and why they matter, and what to do when the model can’t complete the task. They use clear sections, and they grow from observed failures rather than from a brainstorm of hypothetical ones.

Explaining the reason behind a rule generalises better than the rule alone. “Never quote prices” gets followed literally and breaks on the edge case. “Prices change weekly and live in the billing tool, so get them from the tool rather than from memory” lets the model handle cases you didn’t list.

Examples

A few diverse, canonical examples usually beat a long list of rules. Models copy surface features of examples with great fidelity, including length, phrasing, structure and the topics covered. Three examples that all open with “Great question!” will produce a product that opens every answer that way. Vary the examples on every dimension you don’t want copied, and never use eval cases as examples, or your eval stops measuring anything.

Structured outputs

As of October 2026, Anthropic, OpenAI and Google all offer schema-constrained output. The provider restricts generation so the response matches a JSON schema you supply. OpenAI distinguishes this from older JSON mode, which only guarantees valid JSON. Strict tool calling applies the same guarantee to tool arguments.

GuaranteedNot guaranteed
Valid JSON that parsesThat the values are correct
Required fields present, types and enums respectedA schema-shaped answer when the model refuses or hits the output token limit
No retries for format errorsEvery JSON Schema feature (each vendor documents unsupported keywords)

Vendor docs flag practical edges. The first request with a new schema is slower while the grammar is compiled, and the compiled grammar is cached for later calls. Refusals and truncation can return output that doesn’t match the schema, so code must check the stop reason before parsing. Anthropic’s docs also note that changing the output format invalidates the prompt cache for that conversation.

The forced-answer trap

A required field with no escape value forces the model to fill it. If customer_tier is a required enum of three tiers and the input never mentions a tier, you will get a confident guess. Add an explicit unknown or nullable option, and count how often it appears. That count is a quality metric in its own right.

Schema design is product design. Field names and descriptions act as instructions. A short rationale field placed before the decision field can improve the decision and gives reviewers something to read, but keep it brief. Anthropic’s docs warn that asking for long step-by-step reasoning inside a schema field can trigger a refusal.

What changes for you

  • Review system prompt changes like code: every new rule should cite the failure it fixes and the eval case that proves it.
  • Ban eval cases from the example set, and require examples to vary on length, tone and topic.
  • Specify an escape value for every required classification field, and track its rate on the dashboard.
  • Require parsing code to handle refusal and truncation stop reasons explicitly. Schema compliance is a format guarantee only.

lessons.t: Context rot: why more context can make answers worse
lessons.html:
Context windows of hundreds of thousands to around a million tokens invite a simple strategy: put everything in and let the model sort it out. It fails, and the evidence is consistent.

  • Position. Liu et al.’s 2023 paper Lost in the Middle found a U-shaped curve on multi-document question answering. Models used information best when it sat at the beginning or end of the input and noticeably worse when it sat in the middle, including models built for long inputs.
  • Length alone. Chroma’s July 2025 technical report tested 18 models on deliberately simple tasks and found performance grew less reliable as input length increased, often in non-uniform ways. It named the effect context rot.
  • Distractors. In the same report, a single topically related passage that didn’t contain the answer lowered accuracy, and four lowered it further. Models differed in how they failed. Some hallucinated an answer from the distractor; others abstained.
  • Similarity. When the question and the relevant passage shared fewer words and less surface meaning, accuracy fell faster with length. Real user questions rarely echo the wording of your docs.

Anthropic’s engineering guidance frames the cause as an attention budget. Every token added competes for the model’s limited capacity to relate tokens to each other, and models see fewer very long sequences in training. The result is a gradual slope rather than a cliff, which is why it goes unnoticed in demos.

Benchmark claims versus your task

Long-context benchmarks often test retrieval of one distinctive sentence, which is the easiest case. Your task probably has near-duplicate docs, policy versions that differ by one clause, and questions phrased differently from the source. Expect worse than the headline result, and measure it.

Run a length sweep

The practical test is cheap. Take 30 eval cases. For each, build the context at several sizes by padding the relevant material with realistic, related but non-answering content from your own corpus. Plot pass rate against input tokens. The illustrative shape below is common.

Input tokens (illustrative)Pass rateCost per callReading
4k (answer plus 2 neighbours)88%1×Best quality per token
16k86%4×Flat: safe headroom
64k79%16×Degradation visible
200k70%50×Paying more for worse answers

The knee of that curve is your context budget: the largest input that keeps quality within a tolerance you choose, say two points of the best result. Set it well below the advertised window, and re-run the sweep when the model changes, because the curve moves with each model.

Design consequences follow directly. Retrieve fewer, better chunks and rerank them. Remove superseded document versions instead of hoping the model picks the newer one. Summarise old conversation turns. Put the most important instructions and the user’s question where the model attends best, which for long-document tasks usually means documents first and the question last. Give the model a tool to fetch more instead of pre-loading everything it might need.

What changes for you

  • Put a context budget in the spec, derived from a length sweep on your own eval, with a re-test trigger on model change.
  • Push back on “just use the bigger window” proposals until someone shows the sweep.
  • Add distractor cases to the golden set: near-duplicate docs and stale versions that must not win (Chapter 5).

Models are stateless. Everything a chat product or agent appears to remember is context your application chooses to re-send. For a short conversation that is the full history. For a two-hour agent run or a relationship that spans months, it can’t be, because cost grows with every turn and quality falls as context fills (Lesson 3). Each strategy for staying under budget throws something away, and the product question is what you can afford to lose.

StrategyHow it worksWhat it losesFits
Full historyRe-send every turnNothing, until it hits the budgetShort sessions
Sliding windowKeep the last N turns verbatimEarly decisions and constraintsCasual chat
Tool-result clearingReplace old tool outputs with a placeholderRaw data the agent might re-needAgents that read large files or API responses
CompactionSummarise the history and continue in a fresh contextDetail the summary didn’t keepLong agent runs, long working sessions
Structured notesAgent writes progress, decisions and to-dos to a file it re-readsWhatever it didn’t write downMulti-hour tasks, work across sessions
SubagentsDelegate a subtask to a fresh context that returns a short summaryThe subagent’s working detailResearch and search-heavy tasks
Long-term memoryStore facts about the user or project and retrieve them in later sessionsAccuracy, if memories go staleAssistants with returning users

As of October 2026, some of this is moving into the platform. Anthropic’s API, for example, offers server-side compaction, automatic clearing of old tool results once context passes a threshold, and a memory tool the model can write to before content is cleared. Harnesses such as Claude Code compact automatically near the limit. Ask what your stack provides before building it.

Compaction is a lossy summary you must evaluate

The failure is quiet. An agent compacts at turn 60, the summary drops the constraint “don’t touch the billing module”, and at turn 75 it edits the billing module. Anthropic’s guidance is to tune the compaction prompt for recall first (keep everything that might matter) and then trim for precision. Test it directly: plant constraints and decisions early in long synthetic sessions, force a compaction, and check whether the agent still honours them. Track that as its own eval slice.

Caching interacts with all of this

Rewriting or clearing earlier context changes the prefix, so the cached prefix after that point is lost and the next call pays to re-cache. Clear in large batches rather than a little every turn. Lesson 5 explains the cost.

Long-term memory is a product surface

Remembering things across sessions raises questions no summary prompt answers. Which facts get stored, and who decides? Can users see, edit and delete them? How do you stop one user’s memory leaking into another tenant’s context? What happens when a stored fact goes stale, such as a job title from last year? A memory that silently shapes answers and can’t be inspected creates support tickets and privacy reviews. Chapter 9 covers the UX; Chapter 12 covers retention and data handling.

What changes for you

  • Specify the memory policy explicitly: what is kept verbatim, what is summarised, when compaction triggers, and what must always survive it.
  • Add a long-session slice to the eval with planted constraints that must persist through compaction.
  • Treat user-visible memory as a feature with view, edit and delete controls, and get privacy sign-off before launch.

lessons.t: Prompt caching and the economics of a stable prefix
lessons.html:
Every call re-sends its context, and most of that context is identical from call to call. Prompt caching lets the provider store the processed state of an unchanged prefix and reuse it, charging much less for those tokens and cutting time to first token. The match is on an exact prefix. One changed character invalidates the cache from that point onward.

How vendors price it, as of October 2026

VendorHow it is enabledPricing pattern
AnthropicExplicit cache breakpoints on content blocks, or one automatic setting that moves the breakpoint forward as the conversation growsWrites cost a premium over base input (1.25× for the default 5-minute lifetime, 2× for the 1-hour option). Reads cost a small fraction of base input, 10% on most models and lower on some. Minimum cacheable length varies by model.
OpenAIAutomatic by default on supported models; newer models also allow explicit breakpointsNo write premium. Cached reads are discounted heavily, around 90% on recent models. Retention depends on model and data-retention settings.
GoogleImplicit caching on by default for recent Gemini models, plus explicit caches on some modelsSavings applied automatically on implicit hits. Check current docs for rates.

Details change often, so check the docs before you model costs. The method doesn’t change.

A worked example (illustrative)

An agent with a 20,000-token stable prefix (instructions, tool definitions, reference docs) runs 30 calls in a session. Base input price $3 per million tokens. Anthropic-style pricing: writes at 1.25×, reads at 0.1×.

ScenarioPrefix cost per sessionCalculation
No caching$1.8020k × 30 calls × $3/M
Cached, every call within the lifetime$0.25One write (20k × 1.25 × $3/M = $0.075) plus 29 reads (20k × 0.1 × $3/M × 29 = $0.174)
Cached, but users pause past the lifetime every 3rd callAbout $0.8710 writes ($0.75) plus 20 reads ($0.12)

The prefix bill falls by about 86% when the cache stays warm. The third row matters most for product decisions. With frequent pauses, the saving falls to about half. Cache lifetime interacts with user behaviour. A feature people use in bursts caches well; one they return to after lunch may pay the write premium repeatedly, which is when a longer cache lifetime earns its price.

Common cache killers

A timestamp or request ID at the top of the system prompt. The user’s name or plan in the system prompt instead of after it. Tools loaded in a different order per request. Tool sets switched per user segment. A/B tests on system prompt variants, which split traffic across separate caches. Changing the output schema mid-conversation. Each one is a one-line fix once someone looks.

The governing metric is the cache hit rate: cached input tokens divided by total input tokens, read from the usage fields every major API returns. Put it on the feature dashboard next to cost per session. Layout rules follow from the prefix model. Order context from most stable to least stable: tool definitions, system instructions, long reference material, conversation history, then the newest turn. Keep anything per-request or per-user out of the prefix, or place it after a cache breakpoint.

What changes for you

  • Add cache hit rate to the feature dashboard, with a target (for example, above 70% of input tokens for a chat surface) and an alert when it drops.
  • Review prompt and tool changes for cache impact. A one-line edit at the top of the system prompt can raise the bill noticeably.
  • Factor session rhythm into cost models: how often users pause longer than the cache lifetime.

lessons.t: Skills and progressive disclosure: loading context only when needed
lessons.html:
The tension in context design is breadth against focus. You want the agent to know your expense policy, your brand style, your deployment runbook and fifty other procedures. Loading all of them on every call wastes budget and invites context rot. Progressive disclosure resolves this: the model sees a short index of what is available and loads the detail only when a task needs it.

Agent Skills

Agent Skills are the most widely adopted packaging of this idea. A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file whose YAML frontmatter holds a name and a description, followed by instructions, plus optional scripts, reference files and templates. Anthropic developed the format and released it as an open standard at agentskills.io. As of October 2026 it is supported by a long list of agent products, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, Cursor and Gemini CLI.

LevelWhen it loadsCost (Anthropic’s guidance)
Metadata: name and descriptionAlways, at startupAbout 100 tokens per skill
Instructions: the SKILL.md bodyWhen a task matches the descriptionKept under about 5,000 tokens
Resources and scriptsOnly when the instructions point to themNothing until read; a script’s code stays out of context and only its output enters

Fifty skills therefore cost roughly 5,000 tokens of always-on metadata instead of perhaps 200,000 tokens of procedures. Scripts matter as much as the token savings. A validation step done by a script is deterministic and cheap, where asking the model to do it by reasoning is neither.

The description is the trigger

The model decides whether to load a skill by matching the request against its description, so the description must say what the skill does and when to use it. Weak descriptions cause the two characteristic failures: under-triggering (the skill exists but never loads, so the agent improvises) and over-triggering (it loads on loosely related requests and drags irrelevant instructions into context). Both are measurable. Write 20 requests that should trigger the skill and 20 near misses that shouldn’t, and track the trigger rate on each.

Put it in...When
The system promptNeeded on most calls, short, rarely changes
A skillA procedure or body of know-how needed on some tasks, especially with scripts or templates
RetrievalLarge factual corpora where you need a few passages per query (Chapter 7)
A tool or MCP serverLive data or actions in another system (Chapter 6)

Skills and MCP are complementary. MCP gives the agent access to systems; a skill tells it how your team does a task with that access. In many clients, MCP tool definitions load up front, so large tool catalogues have their own context cost.

Skills are software

A skill can instruct the agent to run code and call tools. Anthropic’s docs advise using skills only from trusted sources and auditing every file in one before installing it, as you would any software. Skills that fetch content from external URLs carry the most risk, because fetched content can contain injected instructions (Chapter 12).

What changes for you

  • Ask for an inventory of always-on context and move rarely used procedures into skills or tools.
  • Review skill descriptions as product copy, and require a trigger eval with should-trigger and near-miss cases before a skill ships.
  • Put skills under version control with an owner and review, and route third-party skills through security review.

lab.title: Fix a failing feature with context changes alone
lab.intro: This lab shows how much quality is available without touching the model or its weights. You will hold the model and eval fixed, change only what goes into the context, and keep only the changes the numbers support.
steps: Freeze the setup. Pick one live feature with a known quality problem. Pin the model version, temperature and thinking settings. Use an existing eval of at least 30 cases, or build the 50-case eval from the Chapter 5 lab first. Nothing in this setup changes during the lab.

Record the baseline. Run the eval three times. Record pass rate (mean of the three runs), pass^3 on the critical cases, mean input tokens per call, cache hit rate and p50 latency in the first row of the log below.

Read the assembled context. Dump the full context for five failing cases. Label every slot with its token count and classify each failure as missing, wrong or stale, too much, conflicting, or badly framed (Lesson 1). Count the categories.

Write hypotheses. For the two most frequent categories, write one specific change each and predict its effect on pass rate and tokens. Examples: cut tools from 25 to 8; cap retrieval at 3,000 tokens with reranking; add two varied examples; add an unknown enum value; move per-user fields below the stable prefix.

Change one thing per run. Test at most six variants. Apply each to the baseline (or to the current best, if you are stacking proven changes), run the eval three times, and log it. Keep a change only if the gain exceeds the run-to-run spread you saw in step 2.

Run a length sweep. On the best variant, pad context for 20 cases to roughly 2×, 4× and 8× its current size with realistic, related but non-answering material. Plot pass rate against input tokens and mark the knee as your context budget.

Check the cost side. For the winning configuration, compute cost per call with your provider’s cached and uncached rates, and confirm the cache hit rate did not fall. A quality gain that breaks caching may not be worth it.

Write it up. Fill in the context spec (this chapter’s deliverable) for the winning configuration, attach the log, and list what context alone could not fix. Those items are your case for the next rung of the ladder.

Teams usually find a meaningful gain from cutting irrelevant context alone.

quiz.q: A support assistant answers refund questions wrongly about 20% of the time. The assembled context shows the right policy passage present, ranked 14th of 30 retrieved chunks. What is the best first change?
o: Rewrite the system prompt to emphasise accuracy
Reduce and rerank retrieval so fewer, more relevant chunks reach the model, then re-run the eval
Move to a model with a larger context window
Fine-tune on refund conversations
quiz.w: The information is present but buried among distractors, which is context rot. Smaller, better-ranked retrieval addresses the cause; a bigger window adds more of the same problem.

quiz.q: Your cache hit rate fell from 80% to 15% after a release, and nothing in the system prompt wording changed. Which change most likely caused it?
o: Lowering temperature
Raising max output tokens
Adding the current date and time to the first line of the system prompt
Adding a new eval case
quiz.w: Caching matches an exact prefix. A timestamp at the top changes the prefix on every call, so nothing after it can be reused.

quiz.q: An extraction feature uses structured outputs with a required enum field contract_type. Reviewers find confident but wrong values on documents that don’t state a type. What should you change?
o: Add an explicit unknown option to the enum and track how often it is used
Turn off structured outputs and parse free text
Raise the temperature so the model explores more options
Nothing: structured outputs guarantee correct values
quiz.w: A required field without an escape value forces a guess. Schema compliance guarantees format only, and the rate of unknown becomes a useful metric.

quiz.q: A coding agent follows a “don’t modify the billing module” instruction early in long sessions, then breaks it after about 90 minutes. What is the most likely cause, and the right test?
o: The model is non-deterministic; run at temperature 0
Compaction or history trimming dropped the constraint; add long-session evals with planted constraints that must survive compaction
The system prompt is too short; add more rules
The tool definitions are wrong; rename the tools
quiz.w: Compaction is lossy. Instructions that only live in early turns can disappear from the summary, and planted-constraint tests catch this before users do.

quiz.q: Your team has 60 internal procedures it wants the agent to follow. Putting all of them in the system prompt adds 180,000 tokens. What fits best?
o: Keep them all in the system prompt and rely on caching
Fine-tune the procedures into the model
Package them as skills so only short descriptions load by default and full instructions load when a task matches
Pick the ten most important and drop the rest
quiz.w: Progressive disclosure keeps always-on cost to the metadata, roughly 100 tokens per skill, and loads detail only on demand. Caching cuts cost but not the context rot from 180,000 tokens of mostly irrelevant text.

quiz.q: An engineer proposes A/B testing four system prompt variants at 25% traffic each, for a month. Besides the quality comparison, what should you flag?
o: Four variants need four separate cache prefixes, so cache hit rate and cost per call will worsen during the test
A/B tests are invalid for LLM features
The variants will share a cache and contaminate each other
System prompts can’t be A/B tested because outputs are non-deterministic
quiz.w: Each variant is a different prefix with its own cache. With lower traffic per variant, caches go cold more often, so budget for higher cost and compare cost per variant too.

deliverable.title: Context spec
deliverable.html:
A one-page spec that says exactly what the model sees on each call for one feature, so changes to context are reviewed like changes to code. Keep it in the repo next to the prompt and update it in the same pull request.

  1. Feature and model. Surface, pinned model version, thinking or effort setting, linked eval (Chapter 5).
  2. Slot table. One row per slot, in order: slot name, source (static file, retrieval, tool result, user profile, history), token budget, stable or variable, refresh rule, owner. Mark the cache breakpoint.
  3. Total context budget. The measured knee from the length sweep, the tolerance used, and the date and model it was measured on.
  4. Precedence rules. What wins when the system prompt, retrieved docs, memory and the user disagree.
  5. Output contract. Schema, escape values for every required classification field, and handling of refusal and truncation.
  6. History and memory policy. What is kept verbatim, when compaction triggers, what must survive compaction, what is stored across sessions, and how users view and delete it.
  7. On-demand context. Which skills and tools are available, their descriptions, and the trigger eval results.
  8. Cost and cache. Target cache hit rate, cost per call at median and 95th percentile, and alert thresholds.
  9. Change process. Every change to a slot runs the eval and the cache check before merge.

If a slot has no owner or no budget, that is the first thing to fix.
